blocks.text: Guggenheim 2026: Pixy Liao
It’s never been easy to carry you, 2013 ©Pixy Liao

Over the next few months, we are featuring the work of many of the 2026 Guggenheim Fellows as a way to celebrate their achievements and understand legacies and projects that have brought them this tremendous recognition.

The Board of Trustees of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation announced their appointment of the 101st class of Guggenheim Fellows, including 223 distinguished individuals working across 55 disciplines. Chosen through a rigorous application and peer review process from a pool of nearly 5,000 applicants, the Class of 2026 Guggenheim Fellows was tapped based on both prior career achievement and exceptional promise. As established in 1925 by founder Senator Simon Guggenheim, each Fellow receives a monetary stipend to pursue independent work at the highest level under “the freest possible conditions.”

“Our new class of Guggenheim Fellows is representative of the world’s best thinkers, innovators, and creators in art, science, and scholarship,” said Edward Hirsch, award-winning poet and President of the Guggenheim Foundation. “As the Foundation enters its second century and looks to the future, I feel confident that this new class of 223 individuals will do bold and inspiring work, undaunted by the challenges ahead. We are honored to support their visionary contributions.”
“I open myself to extreme possibilities.” —Pixy Liao

Pixy Liao’s performative tableaux crack into power, sex and gender dynamics in disarming ways. Her work feels naked and tender, serious, yet often laugh out loud funny. She shows us intimacy in natural light and private thoughts played out in familiar domestic spaces. There is delicacy in her color palette and tenderness in her approach, but her work probes deeper.

As she explores her long-term relationship with her boyfriend, Moro, Liao’s work shifts the ways we view what relationships can be. In the series Experimental Relationship , which playfully rearranges the script on art and gender roles, Moro is model and muse, as well as a collaborator with input and agency. She describes her work [with Moro] as “a continuation of our creative partnership and exploration of intimacy through shared performance. I looked at intimacy from a female perspective, how power, desire, and play shift within a couple.”
Relationships work best when each partner knows their proper place, 2008 © Pixy Liao

In her photograph Relationships work best when each partner knows their proper place , a fully clothed Liao pinches Moro’s nipple as he, in turn, squeezes the bulb for the shutter release to take the photo. He is both the model and the mechanism through which she works: the vulnerable nature of collaboration embodied. In these fusions where she and Moro mirror or merge in unexpected ways—giving and taking—she suggests two people can become a unit and be greater together.

Experimental Relationship (2007- Now) As a woman brought up in China, I used to think I could only love someone who is older and more mature than me, who can be my protector and mentor. Then I met my current boyfriend, Moro. Since he is 5 years younger than me, I felt that the whole concept of relationships changed, all the way around. I became a person who has more authority & power. One of my male friends even questioned how I could choose a boyfriend the way a man would choose a girlfriend. And I thought, “Damn right. That’s exactly what I’m doing, & why not!”

I started to seriously think about the significance of this relationship, and start experiments with photographs. My photos explore the alternative possibilities of heterosexual relationships. Moro made me realize that heterosexual relationships don’t need to be standardized. Depending on the individuals, every two people will have a different type of relationship. Even if the relationship is not the type we are familiar with, it still exists and has its own benefits. The purpose of this experiment is to break the inherent relationship model and reach a new equilibrium. Over time, the project also reveals my changing understanding about relationships.
A book “Experimental Relationship Vol.1 2007-2017” was published by Jiazazhi Press in May 2018.
Always Keep an Eye on the One You Love (after ‘Joey the Clown’), 2025 ©Pixy Liao
Channel Your Inner Nude, Stay Fully Dressed, 2025 ©Pixy Liao
Pixy kindly agreed to answer these questions about the Guggenheim for Lenscratch:
What did receiving a Guggenheim Fellowship mean to you at this stage of your career?

PL: Getting the Guggenheim Fellowship was a huge boost for me. Once you’re at this mid-career point, finding support isn’t quite as easy as it was when starting out as an emerging artist. So, having this fellowship lets me take a few bigger risks, try out new things, and hopefully push my work in some fresh directions without worrying so much about what’s next.
Did the fellowship validate something you already knew about your work, or did it change how you see your practice?

PL: It definitely confirmed that exploring the power dynamics in relationships and gender roles strikes a chord on a broader cultural level. For a long time, my creative process has been very intuitive, driven by personal dynamics and genuine honesty with my partner, Moro. Getting the fellowship didn’t necessarily change how I make art, but it gave me a massive vote of confidence. It really strengthened my faith in continuing the “Experimental Relationship” project with Moro for as long as we can, and deepened my conviction that what we’re doing truly matters and has a lasting place in contemporary photography.
How are you using the freedom or access the fellowship provided?

PL: The fellowship gave me a huge sense of mental security, lifting the constant worry about finances. It gave me the breathing room to slow down, dive deeper into new ideas, and experiment with mediums like Risograph and painting that I would usually hesitate to spend time and energy on. We used to limit our photoshoots to times when we traveled for exhibitions so we wouldn’t have to pay for locations out of pocket. Now, with a dedicated budget, we can actually arrange special shoots in the exact locations I envision. Being an artist means constantly juggling logistics and financial weight, so this freedom is invaluable. It’s truly an invitation to be ambitious with my time and focus purely on creation.
What has sustained your practice over the years?

PL:Our work is deeply intertwined with our daily lives, making art and living feel like the exact same thing. What sustains my practice is my relationship with Moro. The fact that we are still together, that he remains entirely supportive, and my endless love of seeing him. As we grow older together, our shared life naturally brings me fresh ideas and ongoing opportunities for the project.
What advice would you give to photographers who are going through the process of applying?

PL: First of all, you need to feel a deep sense of confidence in your own project. This is work you have poured yourself into, are proud of, and know the direction of, and that confidence will naturally show in your application. Beyond confidence, you also need patience. It wasn’t my first time applying, and I’ve always resonated with the idea that fellowships like the Guggenheim often require staying the course until your time comes.

Pixy Liao , originally from Shanghai, China, is an artist based in Tokyo. She has exhibited her work internationally at venues such as Art Institute of Chicago, Fotografiska, Rencontres d’Arles, the Asia Society, and the National Gallery of Australia. Liao is a Guggenheim Fellow and has received the NYFA Fellowship in Photography, the Santo Foundation Individual Artist Award, and the Madame Figaro Women Photographers Award. Her residency history includes Light Work, the Center for Photography at Woodstock, the University of the Arts London, the School of Visual Arts, Pioneer Works, and the Camera Club of New York.
Explore more of Liao’s work at https://www.pixyliao.com/
